info.title: KPOST Communication Platform API
info.description:
REST API surface for the KPOST communication platform: sign-up and login, user profiles, contacts, groups, Katchup messaging, Kall voice/video calling, Kdiary scheduling, Knews, dashboards, admin/company management, and third-party integrations (RedBus, RazorPay, TA Wallet, AWS S3, AI assistants).

**Authentication.** Obtain an access token from `POST /v2/signupLogin/userLogin` and send it as `Authorization: Bearer <accessToken>` on every secured call. Tokens are device-bound: the JWT carries a `deviceID` claim that must match an active row in the login-session table, so a token remains valid only while that device session is alive. An expired access token presented alongside a valid refresh token causes the server to return a freshly minted access token in the `Authorization` response header.

**Response envelope.** Unless documented otherwise, endpoints return a JSON object with `status` (`Success`/`Failure`), `statusCode`, `urlPath` (echoing the route name), and either `msg` or `data` carrying the payload. The HTTP status and the embedded `statusCode` are kept in sync.

tags.name: Company Administration
tags.description:
Privileged company-administration surface: staff provisioning, account lifecycle (hold/release/terminate), role and backup-admin management, and company/bank profile maintenance.

**Access - this is the only role-gated tree in the application.** `SecurityConfiguration` matches `/admin/**` with `.hasRole("admin")`, so every route here requires a bearer token whose principal holds the `admin` authority. A valid token without that role yields **403**, and no token yields **401**. QA should cover both explicitly for each route, since this is the platform's main privilege boundary.

**Acting-admin identity.** Routes that need to record *who* performed an action read the acting admin's `kpostID` from the bearer token and stamp it onto the request object - the payload cannot spoof it. Note, however, that the **target** user or company is generally taken from the request body or path, so the check that an admin may only act within their **own** company is a service-layer responsibility. Cross-company access is the single most important thing to test here: attempt each mutating route against a `companyID` or `kpostID` belonging to a different organisation and confirm rejection.

**Response conventions.** Unusually for this codebase, several routes here return meaningful **400** codes for business validation failures. Two routes are inconsistent: `removeCompanyLogo` and `getBankAndCompanyDetails` set `statusCode` in the body (500 and 404 respectively) that does **not** match the HTTP status actually returned (400 in both cases) - trust the body's `statusCode` for intent and the HTTP status for transport. Every route writes an audit row except `resetPassword` and `holdOrRelease`.

tags.name: Crypto - Payload Encryption Key
tags.description: Publishes the server's RSA public key, which clients use to encrypt request payloads for the routes protected by `PayloadDecryptionFilter`. This is the bootstrap step of the payload-encryption scheme: the client fetches the key once, encrypts its payloads with it, and the filter decrypts them server-side using the matching private key - which never leaves the server.

tags.name: KPresentation
tags.description:
Slide-deck authoring module. Provides create, save, list, fetch and delete operations over presentations owned by the signed-in user, persisted in the MySQL presentation tables.

**Identity.** Ownership is always taken from the `kpostID` on the bearer token; reads and deletes are scoped to it, so a caller cannot reach another user's decks. Every route writes an audit row.

**Response conventions specific to this controller.** Business-level "not found" and "no data" cases are returned as **HTTP 200 with `status=Failure`** rather than 404 - so the HTTP status alone is not sufficient to determine success; always check the `status` field. Genuine exceptions return HTTP 500 with `errorValue`. Note also that several `urlPath` values in the envelope are inconsistent with the actual routes (some carry a leading slash, and the delete route reports an `/api/...` prefix that does not exist) - treat `urlPath` as informational only.

tags.name: User Profile V1 (superseded)
tags.description:
First-generation user-profile surface: search, credentials, privacy, and the education/experience/contact sections of a profile. **Superseded by `/v2/profile`, which is both far larger and materially safer - use that for all new work.**

**Security theme - applies to every route in this controller.** Not one handler here reads the caller's identity from the bearer token. Every route takes the target `kpostID` **from the request body**, and none verifies it against the authenticated principal. `/profile/**` does require authentication (it is not in the `permitAll` list), so a token is needed - but *any* valid token will do. Unless `UserProfileService` independently enforces ownership, that means an authenticated user could read and modify **any other user's** profile, password, access code and privacy settings by supplying their id. This is the single most important thing to test in this controller: for each route, authenticate as user A and target user B, then confirm rejection. The V2 controller resolves identity from the token instead, which is why it supersedes this one.

**Silent-failure theme.** Most handlers have an `if (SUCCESS) { ... }` with **no `else`**. When the service reports anything other than success, nothing is written to the response map and the client receives **HTTP 200 with an empty JSON object `{}`** - no `status`, no message. An empty body is therefore the failure signal on those routes; never treat HTTP 200 as proof the write applied. Affected: `changePassword`, `setProfilePrivacy`, `getUserProfile`, `updateAboutYourself`, `updateContactInformation`, `updateCollegeDetails`, `updateSchoolDetails`, `updateUniversityDetails`, `updateOtherActivity`, `updateExperienceDetails`, `updateBasicInformation`, `updateProfileImage` and `getDigitalCard`.

**Thread-safety.** `resultMap` is a **shared mutable instance field** reassigned by most handlers, so concurrent requests can interleave and responses may be mixed between callers. A genuine defect worth reporting; it also means parallel load runs against a single instance give unreliable results.

**Response conventions.** All routes return a bare `Map` with **HTTP 200 for every outcome** and carry no `statusCode` key; read `status` from the body, and treat an empty body as failure.

tags.name: Kall (Voice/Video) V1 (superseded)
tags.description:
First-generation voice and video calling. **Superseded by `/v2/kall` (`KallControllerV3`), which reworks the model around a `KallMaster` entity with repeat scheduling and explicit member modification.** Note the intermediate `KallControllerV2` is mapped to `unusedv2/kall` and is dead code.

**Two call flavours.** *Direct Kalls* (`initiateKall`, `getKallStatus`, `setKallStatus`) are one-to-one; *Katchup Kalls* (`katchupKall` and the `acceptKatchupKall` / `joinKatchupKall` / `addMemberKatchupKall` / `removeMemberKatchupKall` / `reScheduleKatchupKall` family) are group calls originating from a Katchup conversation, with scheduling and membership of their own.

**Signalling model.** These endpoints manage **call state in MySQL** - they do not carry media. Media flows over the separate VoIP path, and ringing is driven by push notifications (see `/v2/firebase/notificationForKall`), gated by each user's Kall notification preference in General Settings. A call can therefore be correctly recorded here yet never ring, which is the single most common source of confusion when testing this module.

**Identity handling.** Most routes take `HttpServletRequest` and resolve the caller from the bearer token. Two do **not** - `setKallStatus` and `scheduleKall` - so their subject comes entirely from the request body; both are flagged individually.

**Response conventions.** All routes return a bare `Map` with **HTTP 200 for every outcome** - read `status` from the body.

tags.name: KWord Documents
tags.description:
Rich-text document authoring module. Documents are structured as a tree of headings (topics and sub-topics) with content beneath them, persisted in the MySQL KWord tables and owned by the signed-in user.

**Grouping of routes.** Authoring (`create`, `update`, `saveContent`, `deleteHeading`), retrieval (`documentsType`, `documentsType1`, `documents/{docId}`), lifecycle (`delete`, `isConvertToKad`) and collaboration (`share`).

**Identity.** Ownership comes from the `kpostID` on the bearer token - most routes stamp it onto the request DTO or pass it alongside, so a caller cannot act on another user's documents. Every route writes an audit row.

**Response conventions specific to this controller.** "Not found" and "no data" outcomes are returned as **HTTP 200 with `status=Failure` and `statusCode=200`**, never as 404 - so the HTTP status alone cannot be used to detect them; always check `status`. Genuine exceptions return HTTP 500 with `errorValue`. Several `urlPath` values in responses are inaccurate (leading slashes, and `/api/...` prefixes that do not exist on any route) - treat `urlPath` as informational only.

tags.name: Integration - Voice / Speech-to-Text
tags.description: Transcription of voice-note attachments. Resolves a previously uploaded Katchup attachment by its UUID, streams the audio back out of S3 and runs it through the speech-recognition provider to produce a text transcript.

tags.name: User Profile V2
tags.description:
The maintained user-profile surface and the largest controller in the application. Covers: directory search, credentials and access code, privacy settings, the structured profile sections (basic info, contact, school/college/university, experience, activities) each with a save **and** a delete route, profile/cover/signature imagery, digital cards, account deactivation, primary/secondary device management, storage quota and language preferences.

**Identity handling - the key improvement over V1.** Most routes take `HttpServletRequest` and resolve the acting user from the `kpostID` the bearer token supplies, so a caller can only modify their own profile - unlike `/profile`, where every route took the target from the request body. The exceptions are deliberate cross-user reads and are called out individually: `getUserProfileUsingKpostID`, `getUserBasicDetailsUsingKpostID`, `shareUserDetails` and the `download*Image/{kpostID}` routes.

**Public routes.** `SecurityConfiguration` lists these specific paths as `permitAll`, so they are reachable **without a bearer token**: `downloadProfileImage/**`, `downloadFullProfileImage/**`, `downloadCoverImage/**` and `shareUserDetails/**`. Everything else requires authentication.

**Response conventions.** Mostly the typed `ApiResponse<T>` envelope (`statusCode`, `status`, `message`, `urlPath`, `data`) with accurate HTTP codes. Some routes return raw `Map`, and the image download routes return **raw bytes**; these are noted individually.

tags.name: Kall (Voice/Video) V2 - current
tags.description:
**The maintained voice and video calling surface.** Note the naming: the class is `KallControllerV3` but it is mapped to **`/v2/kall`**, because the intermediate `KallControllerV2` was abandoned and renamed to `unusedv2/kall`. Clients should use `/v2/kall`.

**What changed from V1.** The model is reorganised around a `KallMaster` entity with a richer request object (`KallROV3`), adding: **repeat scheduling** (`scheduledRepeatKall`, `fetchScheduledRepeatKall`), explicit **membership modification** (`modifyKallMembers` alongside `addMembersToKall`), per-participant call termination (`endIndividualKall` as well as `endKoolKall`), and richer status reads (`getKallStatus`, `getKallStatusUsingKallID`, `updateSenderAndReceiverKallStatus`). Several routes now carry `@Valid`, so malformed payloads produce genuine **400** responses rather than being swallowed.

**Signalling only.** As in V1, these endpoints manage **call state in MySQL** and do not carry media. Ringing is driven by VoIP push, gated by each user's Kall notification preference in General Settings, so a call can be correctly recorded here yet never ring - the most common source of confusion when testing this module.

**Identity handling.** Every route takes `HttpServletRequest` and resolves the caller from the bearer token - a deliberate correction of V1, where `setKallStatus` and `scheduleKall` took no caller identity at all. What the service must still enforce per route is that the caller is a participant in the call they are acting on; that is the recurring authorisation test here.

**Response conventions.** Mostly `ResponseEntity<Map>` with `status`, `statusCode`, `urlPath` and `data`; a few routes return a bare `Map`. Business-level "no rows" outcomes are often reported as **HTTP 500** rather than an empty 200. Every route writes an audit row.

tags.name: TA Wallet Payments
tags.description:
Payment initiation and gateway callback handling for the TA Wallet provider, used by the KBooking flow.

**Two distinct audiences.** `createHash` and `fetchTransactionDetailsByOrderId` are JSON APIs called by the KPOST client; `paymentRequest` and `paymentRequest1` are **browser-facing gateway callbacks** that accept `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` posts from the payment provider and reply with HTML or a 302 redirect rather than JSON. Do not send JSON to the callback routes.

**Access.** The whole `/taWallet/**` tree is `permitAll` in `SecurityConfiguration` - no bearer token is required, because the gateway cannot present one. Integrity rests on the salted hash rather than on session authentication.

**Note:** this class is a plain `@Controller`; the JSON routes are individually marked `@ResponseBody`. All four routes are `@Transactional`. It also shares the `/taWallet` base path with `TAWalletIntegrationController`.

tags.name: Common Reference Data & Utilities V2
tags.description:
The maintained shared-services surface, and a strict superset of `/common`. Groups into: **reference lookups** (countries, professions, designations, languages, domains, states, cities, postal codes), **OTP flows** for mobile and email, **password recovery**, **company lookups and enquiry capture**, **app-version management**, and a handful of utilities including a Katchup send bridge and company-logo upload/download.

**Access - important.** The whole `/v2/common/**` tree is `permitAll` in `SecurityConfiguration`, so **every route here is reachable without a bearer token**. That is necessary for the registration and recovery flows, but it also means the company lookups, user lookups and the `sendMessage` bridge are unauthenticated. Several of these are user-enumeration primitives (`mobileNoExist`, `getUserDetailsByMobNo`, `uniqueNameExist`, `isCompanyNameExist`); QA should check whether they are rate-limited, because without throttling the platform's user and company base can be enumerated. The individual operations flag the higher-risk cases.

**Response conventions.** Mostly the typed `ApiResponse<T>` envelope (`statusCode`, `status`, `message`, `urlPath`, `data`) with accurate HTTP codes - a marked improvement over V1's untyped maps. A minority of routes still return raw `Map` or specialised types (`msStatus` returns a bare string, `downloadCompanyLogo` returns image bytes); those are called out individually.

tags.name: Integration - AWS S3 Pre-signed URLs
tags.description:
Direct-to-S3 attachment handling. Rather than streaming large files through the application, clients ask this module for a short-lived pre-signed **PUT** URL, upload the bytes straight to S3, then call back to confirm the object landed.

**Typical flow.** (1) `generate-presigned-url` (GET or POST) or `katchup/generate-presigned-url` returns a signed URL. (2) The client `PUT`s the file to that URL directly - that request goes to AWS, not to KPOST. (3) `checkAttachmenS3/{uuid}` (single) or `checkAttachmentS3` (batch) verifies the object exists. (4) `deleteAttachmentFromS3/{uuid}` removes it if the user cancels.

**Identity and isolation.** The target bucket comes from server configuration (`jsa.s3.bucket`) and is never accepted from the client. The caller's `kpostID` is taken from the bearer token and used to scope the object key, which is how one user's attachments are kept out of another's namespace - the check and delete routes reject UUIDs that do not belong to the caller.

**Response conventions specific to this controller.** The three URL-generation routes return a **bare string** (the signed URL), not a JSON envelope. The verification routes use an unusually wide spread of HTTP codes (406, 417, 404) to distinguish upload outcomes - see each operation. Every route writes an audit row.

tags.name: Groups V2
tags.description:
The maintained group-management surface. Extends the V1 operations (create, add/remove members, admin delegation, leave) with group imagery, renaming, detail lookup and deletion.

**Identity handling.** Every route stamps the acting user from the bearer token - `groupAdmin` on the admin-facing routes, `kpostID` on `leaveFromGroup` and `deleteGroup` - so the payload cannot spoof who is acting. What the service must still enforce is that this actor genuinely administers the target group; that is the recurring authorisation test across the whole controller.

**Public routes.** `downloadGroupProfileImage/**` and `downloadGroupFullProfileImage/**` are listed as `permitAll` in `SecurityConfiguration`, so group avatars are retrievable **without a bearer token**. Both take a `kpostID` path segment in addition to the group id - see their notes.

**Response conventions.** `ResponseEntity<Map>` with `status`, `statusCode`, `urlPath` and `data`. Several routes have **no `else` branch**, so a non-success service result yields **HTTP 200 with an empty body `{}`** rather than an error - treat an empty body as failure. Failure envelopes use `errorCode` (a description, not a code). Every route writes an audit row.

tags.name: Integration - RedBus Bus Booking
tags.description:
Bus search and ticketing, implemented as a proxy over the RedBus (Seat Seller) partner API. Almost every route here makes a live outbound call to RedBus through `SSRestServiceClient`, authenticated with the server-held `apiRedBusConsumerKey` / `apiRedBusConsumerSecret` - those credentials are never accepted from or returned to the client.

**Booking journey, in order.** `citysuggestion/{cityname}` → `destinations` → `availabletrips` → `tripdetails` (or `tripdetailsV2`) → `boardingPoint` → `seatLayout` → `getUpdatedFare` → `blockTicket/{kPostId}` → payment via the RazorPay module → `bookticket` → `ticketdetails`. `checkBookedTicket`, `getTicket` and `cancelticket` serve the post-booking lifecycle. Steps are stateful: a trip id from `availabletrips` is required by the detail calls, and a block id from `blockTicket` is required to complete `bookticket` before it expires.

**Side effects and money.** `blockTicket`, `bookticket` and `cancelticket` mutate real inventory at RedBus and have financial consequences. Exercise them only against RedBus test credentials, never a production key.

**QA notes for the whole controller.** Latency and failure modes are dominated by the upstream partner, so build in generous timeouts and treat upstream outages as expected 5xx conditions rather than defects. Three routes (`boardingPoint`, `checkBookedTicket`, `getTicket`) are declared with a bare `@RequestMapping` and therefore respond to **every** HTTP method, not just POST. Note also that this controller holds its `resultMap` in a **shared instance field** that each handler reassigns; under concurrent requests that field is not thread-safe, so avoid drawing conclusions from parallel load runs against a single instance.

tags.name: Authentication - Medium & Large Enterprise
tags.description:
Registration and login for the medium/large enterprise tier, where accounts belong to a company and are typically provisioned by a company administrator rather than self-registered.

**Access.** The `/signupLoginForMediumAndLarge/**` tree is listed as `permitAll` in `SecurityConfiguration`, so these routes are reachable without a bearer token - which is what makes them usable for genuine registration and login, unlike the V1 `/signupLogin` tree.

**Auditing.** Every route writes an audit row; note `signup` and `adminUserLogin` audit against the mobile number and kpostID from the payload rather than an authenticated identity, since no token exists at that point.

**Response conventions.** `signup` returns a bare `Map` with HTTP 200 for all outcomes, while `addingUserByAdmin` and `adminUserLogin` return real `ResponseEntity` values with meaningful status codes - `adminUserLogin` in particular uses the typed `LoginApiResponse` envelope and is the only route in this controller with genuine bean-validation-driven **400** handling.

tags.name: Kdiary - Schedules, Events & Reports
tags.description:
The Kdiary planner module. Covers three related record types, all persisted through the MySQL diary-schedule tables:

- **Schedules** - the day-plan entries a user creates for themselves (`createSchedule`, `getTodaySchedules`, `updateScheduleRemarks`).
- **Events** - calendar entries that may carry participants (`createEvent`, `updateEvent`, `getEvents`, `getEventDate`, `getEventSelectedDate`, `deleteEvent`, `addparticipants`, `editScheduleEvent`).
- **Reports** - the daily activity report attached to a date (`saveReport`, `editReport`, `deleteReport`, `getTodayReport`).

**Note the base path is `/dairySchedule`** - the misspelling of "diary" is part of the deployed contract and must be reproduced exactly.

**Identity handling.** Ownership is always taken from the `kpostID` on the bearer token, never from the request body: the create/edit routes overwrite `createdBy`/`kpostID` server-side, and the read routes scope their queries to the token identity. Every route writes an audit row.

**Response conventions specific to this controller.** A handled business failure returns `status=Failure` with **HTTP 500**, while an unhandled exception returns `status=Error` (not `Failure`) also with 500 - so 500 here does not reliably mean "server fault". Empty result sets are likewise reported as 500 rather than an empty 200.

tags.name: Kall V2 (abandoned - base path 'unusedv2/kall')
tags.description:
**An abandoned intermediate iteration of the Kall module. The base path is literally `unusedv2/kall` - the authors renamed it to take it out of service rather than deleting the code.**

**Status.** These routes are still mapped and will respond if called, because Spring registers them like any other handler and `/unusedv2/kall/**` falls under `anyRequest().authenticated()` - so they are reachable by any authenticated user. No shipping client should call them: the live surfaces are `/kall` (V1) and `/v2/kall` (V3, in `KallControllerV3`).

**Why it is documented at all.** It is included for completeness of the deployed contract, and because dead-but-reachable endpoints are a genuine risk: they duplicate business logic that no longer receives review or fixes, and any security defect corrected in V1 or V3 may still be present here. Several of the concerns flagged on the V1 controller - notably `setKallStatus` taking no caller identity - are reproduced verbatim in this copy.

**Recommendation for QA.** Rather than writing functional coverage for these routes, verify they are unreachable in production (confirm no client calls `unusedv2/*`) and raise their **removal** as a ticket. If they must stay, they need the same security review as the live controllers. Behaviour otherwise mirrors the correspondingly named V1 routes; the notable additions are `todayKoolKall` and the absence of V1's `scheduleKall` and `getKallHistory`.

**Response conventions.** As V1: a bare `Map` with **HTTP 200 for every outcome** - read `status` from the body.

tags.name: Integration - E-commerce Catalogue
tags.description: Read-only reference data describing the e-commerce partners and platforms surfaced inside KPOST. Both routes are lookup endpoints backed by MySQL reference tables and are safe to cache client-side.

tags.name: Katchup Messaging V1 (superseded)
tags.description:
First-generation Katchup messaging: send, fetch, recall, flag, delete and search. **Superseded by `/v2/katchup`, which is far larger - it adds attachments, media streaming, forwarding, bulk send and abuse reporting - and should be used for all new work.**

**Mixed identity handling.** Most routes stamp the acting user from the bearer token, which is correct. Two do **not** take `HttpServletRequest` at all - `recallMessage` and `getReadStatusGroupMessage` - so their subject comes entirely from the request body with no ownership check. `recallMessage` is the serious one, since recall deletes a message from the recipient's device; see its note.

**Thread-safety.** `resultMap` is declared as a shared mutable instance field. Most handlers shadow it with a local variable, but `getUnopenedMessagesCount1` assigns to the **field**, so concurrent requests can interleave there - responses may be mixed between callers under load.

**Response conventions.** Mostly a bare `Map` returned with **HTTP 200 for every outcome** - read `status` from the body. `sendMessage` is the exception, returning a real `ResponseEntity` with a genuine 400. `status` is `Success`, `Failure` or `Error` (the last reserved for caught exceptions). Most routes write an audit row.

tags.name: Katchup Messaging V2
tags.description:
The maintained messaging surface and the largest controller in the application. Groups into: **sending** (plain, multipart-with-attachments, bulk, and draft save), **reading** (thread fetch, subjects, unread counts, deleted-id sync), **message actions** (recall, delete, flag important, change caption, report abuse), **forwarding** (four variants with reference back-tracking), **attachments** (upload, five download routes, thumbnails, media streaming) and **search/filter**.

**Identity handling.** Every route takes `HttpServletRequest` and resolves the sender or reader from the `kpostID` on the bearer token, so a caller cannot spoof message authorship - a deliberate contrast with `POST /v2/common/sendMessage`, which takes both sender and receiver from the body on an unauthenticated route.

**Public routes.** `downloadThumbnail/**` and `downloadAttachment/**` are listed as `permitAll` in `SecurityConfiguration`, so those two are reachable **without a bearer token** - see their notes, since attachment content is private message data.

**Message types.** The platform encodes message semantics as integers on the message row: 0 normal, 1 reply, 2 share, 3 reminder, 4 SMS, 5 note, 6 edit, 7 recall, 8 comment, 9 clarify, 10 mail notification, 11 group notification, 14 copies, 15 forward, 17 schedule-Kall notification, 25 share document. Several routes below behave differently by type.

**Response conventions.** Mostly `ResponseEntity<Map>` with `status`, `statusCode`, `urlPath` and `data`; business-level "no rows" outcomes are frequently reported as **HTTP 500** rather than an empty 200. The download and streaming routes return **raw bytes**, and `changeCaption` returns a bare **string**. Every route writes an audit row.

tags.name: Knews
tags.description:
The in-app news module. Splits into two groups: **reference lookups** (categories, sub-categories, publications, sources) that feed the news-preferences picker, and the **per-user settings** pair that stores which of those a user has subscribed to.

**Response conventions specific to this controller.** An empty result set is reported as **HTTP 404** with `status=Failure` rather than an empty 200, and an unhandled exception yields `status=Error` with `errorValue` carrying the exception text (note: `Error`, not the usual `Failure`). The settings routes always act on the `kpostID` resolved from the bearer token - any `kpostId` in the body is overwritten.

tags.name: Integration - AI Assistant
tags.description:
Conversational AI assistant embedded in KPOST. Supports multiple upstream providers selected per request via `aiType` (defaulting to `deepseek`), maintains persistent chat sessions per user, and offers both buffered and streaming (SSE) response modes.

**Sessions.** Conversations are stored in MySQL against the caller's `kpostID`, grouped into sessions identified by `sessionId`. Omitting `sessionId` on `chatResponse` starts a new session; supplying one continues an existing conversation with its prior context.

**Identity.** Every route derives `kpostID` from the bearer token and scopes session reads to it, so a caller cannot enumerate another user's conversations.

**Response conventions specific to this controller.** `status` is uppercase here (`SUCCESS`, `ERROR`, `QUOTA_EXCEEDED`) rather than the platform-standard `Success`/`Failure`, failure bodies use `message` rather than `msg`, and upstream quota exhaustion surfaces as a genuine **HTTP 429**. Every route writes an audit row.

tags.name: General Settings
tags.description: Per-user application preferences: display personalisation (font size and theme) and the per-module notification switches for Katchup, Kmail and Kall. Every route in this controller acts on the caller identified by the `kpostID` request attribute that `AuthenticationFilter` derives from the bearer token - the user is never taken from the request body, so one user can never change another user's settings. Reads and writes target the MySQL general-settings and notification-preference tables.

tags.name: Authentication V2
tags.description:
The maintained sign-up, login and session-management surface. All clients should use these routes rather than the V1 `/signupLogin` equivalents.

**Access.** The whole `/v2/signupLogin/**` tree is `permitAll` in `SecurityConfiguration`, so the routes are reachable without a bearer token. That is required for registration and login, but note it also means the token-reading routes here (`getActiveSession`, `userLogout`, `userLogoutFromAllDevices`, `getLoginHistory`) are **not** enforced by the filter chain - they instead read the `kpostID` request attribute, which `AuthenticationFilter` only populates when a valid token *was* presented. Calling them without a token yields a null identity, which each route handles differently; `userLogoutFromAllDevices` is the only one that explicitly returns **401**.

**Token model.** `userLogin` mints a JWT carrying `kpostID`, `deviceID` and `companyID` claims and opens a row in the login-session table. `AuthenticationFilter` validates both the signature and that the token's `deviceID` still has a live session, so revoking a session immediately invalidates its token. `generateJWTokens` exchanges a refresh token for a fresh access token.

**Response conventions.** Mixed by design: `userLogin` uses the typed `LoginApiResponse` envelope with accurate status codes, `signup` returns a bare `Map` at HTTP 200 for all outcomes, and the remainder return `ResponseEntity` maps that report business-level failures - including "no rows found" - as **HTTP 500**. Treat 500 on the read routes as "empty", not necessarily as a fault.

tags.name: Dashboard V2
tags.description:
Aggregated activity feeds that populate the KPOST home screen and the per-module landing screens for Katchup, Kall and Kmail. These are the highest-traffic read endpoints in the platform and are designed for incremental sync: the client sends the highest identifier it already holds and receives only newer records plus a fresh cursor.

**Identity handling (applies to every route here).** The recipient is always overwritten server-side from the `kpostID` claim on the bearer token - any `receiver` / `kpostUser` value sent in the request body is discarded. A caller therefore cannot read another user's dashboard by spoofing the payload, and QA should not expect that field to influence the result.

**Auditing.** Every call writes an audit row via `AuditService.logAudit` keyed on the route name.

tags.name: Firebase Diagnostics
tags.description: Diagnostic harness for the Firebase Cloud Messaging pipeline that delivers Kall push notifications. Intended for engineering and QA verification of device-token registration and FCM connectivity - it is not part of the normal client call flow, which receives Kall pushes as a side effect of the `/v2/kall` endpoints.

tags.name: Integration - RazorPay Payments
tags.description:
RazorPay payment flow backing the RedBus ticket booking journey. Two steps: `generateOrderId` creates a RazorPay order server-side and links it to a pending booking, then - after the user completes checkout in the RazorPay widget - `validateAndUpdateTransactionDetails` cryptographically verifies the gateway's signature before the payment is recorded as genuine.

**Secrets.** The RazorPay key and secret are held server-side (`razor.key`, `razor.secret`) and are never accepted from or returned to the client. Signature verification uses the secret, which is what makes the confirmation step trustworthy - a client cannot forge a successful payment.

**Response conventions specific to this controller.** Gateway-side failures return **HTTP 424 Failed Dependency**, which is unusual for this codebase. Both routes talk to a live third-party payment gateway, so exercise them against RazorPay test credentials only.

tags.name: Contacts Directory V2
tags.description:
The maintained contacts surface. Covers the four incremental-sync listings that populate the app's contact and group pickers (`myContacts`, `myUnknownKatchupContacts`, `myGroups`, `myUnknownGroups`), plus contact creation (single and bulk), phone-book import, blocking (single and bulk), search, invitations and deletion.

**Identity handling - the improvement over V1.** Almost every route takes `HttpServletRequest` and resolves the acting user from the bearer token, so listings are caller-scoped and writes land in the caller's own directory. `getSearchDetails` is the one route that still omits it - see its note.

**"Known" vs "unknown" contacts.** KPOST distinguishes contacts a user has explicitly added from counterparties they have only exchanged messages with. The `myUnknown*` routes surface the latter so the client can offer to add them; the plain routes return the saved directory.

**Incremental sync.** The four listing routes accept a `ContactsRO` carrying a last-sync marker and return only records changed since, which is what keeps the client's local database current. Sending an empty marker degenerates to a full fetch.

**Response conventions.** `ResponseEntity<Map>` with `status`, `statusCode`, `urlPath` and `data`. Business-level "no rows" outcomes are frequently reported as **HTTP 500** rather than an empty 200, so treat 500 on the read routes as "empty" rather than a fault.

tags.name: Integration - MetaDee AI
tags.description: Proxy to the external MetaDee / Lumina generative-AI service. This module forwards a user prompt to the third-party endpoint configured by `apiUrlForMetaDee` and returns the generated completion. The route is registered as `permitAll` in the security chain, so it is reachable without a bearer token; every call is still recorded by the audit service against the caller's IP and URI.

tags.name: Groups V1 (superseded)
tags.description:
First-generation group management: creation, membership and admin delegation. **Superseded by `/v2/group`, which adds group imagery, renaming, deletion and detail lookup on top of these operations.**

**Identity handling - correct here.** Unlike `UserProfileController` V1, every route in this controller stamps the acting user from the bearer token: `groupAdmin` on the admin-facing routes and `kpostID` on `leaveFromGroup`. The payload therefore cannot spoof who is acting, and the service is given a trustworthy actor to authorise against. What each route still needs to enforce at the service layer is that this actor genuinely administers the target group - that is the recurring test.

**Response conventions.** All routes return a bare `Map` with **HTTP 200 for every outcome**, carrying no `statusCode` and no `urlPath`. Notably, `status` is often set to the raw service return value rather than a normalised constant, so it is not always `Success`/`Failure`. Failure envelopes use `errorCode` (a description, not a code) plus `errorValue` (the exception text). Read `status` from the body; never rely on the HTTP status.

**Note.** A sixth route, `getGroupDetails`, is commented out in the source with the note that the client now keeps group details in a local database; use `GET /v2/group/getGroupDetailsUsingGroupKpostID/{groupKpostID}` instead.

tags.name: Contacts Directory V1 (superseded)
tags.description:
First-generation contacts management: phone-book import, contact references, blocking, search and deletion. **Superseded by `/v2/contacts`, which is a superset - use that for all new work.**

**Mixed identity handling.** Some routes correctly stamp `kpostID` from the bearer token (`addContactReference`, `blockOrUnBlockContact`, `deleteContact`, `getblockContactDetails`); others take the subject **from the request body** with no ownership check (`importPhoneContacts`, `getImportedPhoneContacts`, `getSearchDetails`, `contactAllDetails`). The body-driven ones are flagged individually - `getImportedPhoneContacts` is the most serious, since a phone book is bulk personal data belonging to a third party.

**Two broken routes.** `katchupContacts` is declared `@GetMapping` but annotates its `HttpServletRequest` parameter with `@RequestBody`, which is not a valid binding - see its note. `globalSearch` has its entire implementation commented out and always returns an empty object.

**Response conventions.** All routes return a bare `Map` with **HTTP 200 for every outcome** and no `statusCode` key. `status` is `Success`, `Failure` or `Error` (the last reserved for caught exceptions). Failure envelopes mix `errorMsg`, `errorValue`, `errorcode` and `errorvalue` inconsistently - read `status` first.

tags.name: Integration - TA Wallet Callback
tags.description: Inbound callback surface used by the TA Wallet partner system to push communication messages into KPOST. Shares the `/taWallet` base path with the payment endpoints in `TAWalletController` and is registered as `permitAll` in the security chain.

tags.name: Authentication V1 (superseded)
tags.description:
First-generation sign-up, login and session management. **Superseded by `/v2/signupLogin` - use that for all new work.**

**Critical access note.** Unlike its V2 successor, the `/signupLogin/**` tree is **not** listed among the `permitAll` matchers in `SecurityConfiguration`, so every route here - including `signup` and `userLogin` - falls under `anyRequest().authenticated()` and requires a valid bearer token. That makes the registration and login routes unreachable for the very callers who need them (a user with no account has no token), which is the main reason this controller is effectively dead. QA should expect **401** on these routes unless a token is supplied.

**Known defect affecting two routes.** `setAccessCode` and `userLogout` read the request attribute `"kpostId"`, but `AuthenticationFilter` writes `"kpostID"` (capital D). The lookup therefore always returns **null** and the caller identity is silently lost - see the individual operations.

**Response conventions.** All routes return a bare `Map` with **HTTP 200 regardless of outcome**; success or failure must be read from the `status` field in the body. There is no `statusCode` key on most responses. Failure envelopes mix `msg`, `errorMsg` and `errorValue` inconsistently.

tags.name: Common Reference Data V1 (superseded)
tags.description:
First-generation reference-data and OTP surface: country/language/profession/designation lookups and the mobile and email OTP flows. **Superseded by `/v2/common`, which is a strict superset - use that instead.**

**Critical access note.** Unlike `/v2/common/**`, the `/common/**` tree is **not** listed among the `permitAll` matchers in `SecurityConfiguration`, so every route here falls under `anyRequest().authenticated()` and requires a valid bearer token. That makes the registration-support routes - `sendOTP`, `validateOTP`, `mobileNoExist`, `countries` - unreachable for the unauthenticated callers who actually need them during sign-up, which is why the V2 tree exists. Expect **401** on these routes without a token.

**Thread-safety note.** This controller stores `resultMap` as a **shared mutable instance field** that most handlers reassign and populate. Under concurrent load two requests can interleave on that field, so responses may be mixed between callers. Do not draw conclusions from parallel load runs against a single instance, and treat this as a genuine defect worth reporting. The handlers that declare a local `resultMap` (`validateOTP`, `mobileNoExist`, `sendOTPtoMail`, `validateMailOTP`) are unaffected.

**Response conventions.** All routes return a bare `Map` with **HTTP 200 regardless of outcome** - read `status` from the body. There is no `statusCode` key anywhere in this controller, and failures mix `msg`, `errorMsg` and `errorValue` inconsistently.

tags.name: Dashboard V1 (superseded)
tags.description: Legacy dashboard routes retained for backwards compatibility with older mobile builds. **These handlers are no longer wired to the dashboard service - the service invocations are commented out in the source, so both routes are live but perform no query and return no data.** All current clients must use the `/v2/dashboard` equivalents, which are the maintained implementations. Documented here so the published contract matches the deployed behaviour and QA does not write assertions against data these routes cannot return.

post.summary: Transcribe a voice-note attachment to text
post.description:
Converts an already-uploaded voice attachment into a plain-text transcript.

**Business purpose.** Lets recipients read a voice note instead of playing it, and feeds searchable text for voice messages inside Katchup.

**Flow.** (1) `uuid` from the request body is looked up in the MySQL `katchup_attachment` table via `KatchupAttachmentRepository.findByUuid` to resolve the stored `filePath` and `s3FileName`. (2) The binary is streamed back from AWS S3 through `AWSs3ClientService.multiPartfileNewDownload`. (3) The stream is handed to `SpeechService.speechToText`, which calls the speech-recognition provider and returns the transcript as a bare string (not the usual JSON envelope).

**Side effects.** Read-only against KPOST data; consumes S3 egress and speech-provider quota.

**QA notes.** The success body is a raw `text/plain`-style string, not a JSON envelope - assert on the string content directly. A UUID that exists in the request but not in `katchup_attachment` causes a `NullPointerException` on `getFilePath()` and surfaces as HTTP 500; a UUID whose S3 object is missing raises `Failed to download file from S3`, also surfacing as 500.

requestBody.description: Attachment selector. Only the `uuid` field is read; all other `KatchupAttachment` fields are ignored.

500.description: The UUID did not resolve to a stored attachment, the S3 object could not be downloaded, or the speech provider failed.

200.description: Audio was transcribed successfully. The body is the raw transcript text.

schema.example: please move tomorrow's review to four o clock

The response envelope carries `status=Failure` and a `msg` naming the offending field.

Re-authenticate to obtain a new token.

post.summary: Log out of a device session
post.description:
Ends the login session for a single device, immediately invalidating the token bound to it. This is the working replacement for the defective V1 `userLogout`.

**Flow.** The handler overwrites `kpostID` on the request object with the value resolved from the bearer token - correctly using the `"kpostID"` attribute, unlike V1, which reads `"kpostId"` and always gets null. `SignUpLoginService.userlogout` then deletes the matching row from the MySQL login-session table and returns the number of rows affected; success requires `result > 0`. An audit row is written.

**Side effects.** Deletes a session row. Because `AuthenticationFilter` checks each request's token `deviceID` against that table, the token for that device stops authenticating immediately and subsequent calls return 401. Irreversible - the device must sign in again.

**QA notes.** The identity is taken from the token, so the `deviceID` in the body selects **which of the caller's own sessions** to end; confirm that supplying another user's `deviceID` does not revoke their session, since the delete should be scoped by both values. Omitting `deviceID` matches no row and yields the **HTTP 500** empty case. The definitive assertion is behavioural: after logout, reuse the revoked token and expect **401**, and confirm the device disappears from `getActiveSession`. As with the sibling routes, this tree is `permitAll`, so calling without a token gives a null identity and the 500 path rather than a 401.

requestBody.description: Identifies which device session to end. Any `kpostID` supplied here is ignored and overwritten from the bearer token.

200.description: Session ended. Envelope carries `status=Success`, `statusCode=200` and `msg="You have been successfully logged out!"`.

500.description: No matching session was removed - unknown or omitted `deviceID`, a session already ended, or no authenticated identity. Envelope carries `status=Failure` and `statusCode=500`.

The response envelope carries `status=Failure` and a `msg` naming the offending field.

Re-authenticate to obtain a new token.

post.summary: Authenticate a user and issue access/refresh tokens
post.description:
**The primary login endpoint for the platform.** Validates credentials and, on success, issues the JWT access token and opens a device-bound login session.

**Flow.** Bean validation runs first: if `BindingResult` reports errors the handler short-circuits with **HTTP 400** carrying the first field error's message. Otherwise an audit row is written against the payload's `kpostID`, and `SignUpLoginServiceV2.userSignupLoginValidate` resolves the user from the MySQL user table, verifies the credential, inserts a row into the login-session table keyed by `deviceID`, and mints a JWT carrying `kpostID`, `deviceID` and `companyID`. The method is `@Transactional`, so a failure part-way rolls the session write back.

**Side effects.** Creates a login-session row and may supersede an existing session for the same device. Failed attempts may feed lockout counters. Writes an audit row.

**Access.** `permitAll` - no bearer token required.

**QA notes.** This is the setup step for essentially every other test in the suite: capture `data.accessToken` and send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `deviceID` is effectively mandatory - `AuthenticationFilter` matches the token's `deviceID` claim against the session table on every subsequent request, so a token minted without one authenticates nothing. Two behaviours worth targeting: (1) all non-validation failures, **including wrong credentials**, collapse into HTTP 500 with `message="API service is not working"`, so that message does not distinguish a bad password from an outage - assert on the absence of a token instead; (2) the success path calls `responseObject.getBody()` without a null check, so a service returning an empty body would NPE into that same 500.

requestBody.description: Credentials plus the device identity the session is bound to. Subject to bean validation.

500.description: Login could not be completed - covers rejected credentials as well as genuine faults. Envelope carries `message="API service is not working"`.

200.description: Authenticated. The `LoginApiResponse` body carries the access token, refresh token and user summary.

400.description: Bean validation failed on the login payload. Envelope carries `statusCode=400`, `status=Failure` and `message` set to the first offending field's validation message.

401.description: Unauthorized - the `Authorization` header is missing or malformed, the JWT signature is invalid, the access token has expired with no usable refresh token, or the token's `deviceID` claim no longer matches an active login session (for example after a logout from all devices). Re-authenticate to obtain a new token.

403.description: Forbidden - the caller is authenticated but lacks the authority for this route. Applies to `/admin/**` routes that require the `admin` role, and to resource-level checks such as acting on a group the caller does not administer or on a message the caller does not own.

post.summary: Register a new KPOST user
post.description:
**The primary registration endpoint.** Creates a KPOST account after applying a substantial set of controller-level validations.

**Defaulting.** Two fields are defaulted before validation rather than rejected: an empty `gender` becomes `"others"`, and an empty `dateOfBirth` becomes `"1990-01-01"`. Clients that omit a real date of birth therefore silently receive that placeholder - worth knowing when asserting stored profile data.

**Validation gate.** Registration proceeds only if **all** hold: `kpostID` non-empty, contains no space, contains no run of 2+ consecutive whitespace characters, and has a non-empty local part before `@`; `firstName` and `lastName` non-empty after trimming; `password` non-empty after trimming; `gender` is one of `male`, `female` or `others` (case-insensitive). Additionally, when `userType` is `PERSONAL`, the local part of `kpostID` (before `@`) must be **4-12 characters** - this length rule applies only to personal accounts. Any failure returns the single generic message `"Enter valid Credentials"`, which does not identify which rule failed.

**Flow.** On passing, `SignUpLoginService.singup` checks uniqueness, hashes the credential and inserts the user, profile and default-settings rows into MySQL.

**Side effects.** Creates persistent account records and typically triggers the welcome SMS/email path. Not idempotent. Writes an audit row.

**Access.** `permitAll` - no bearer token required.

**QA notes.** This returns a **bare `Map` with HTTP 200 for every outcome** - including failures, which carry `statusCode=500` *inside the body*. Never assert on the HTTP status; read `status` and `statusCode` from the body. Two null-safety risks to target: `getFirstName()`, `getLastName()` and `getPassword()` are `.trim()`-ed **before** any null check, so omitting any of those three throws an NPE caught as `status=Error`; and the `substring(0, indexOf("@"))` guard throws if `kpostID` contains no `@` at all. In both cases the response is `status=Error` with **no** `errorMsg` key, which is the least diagnosable failure in the module. Note also that the `CONSECUTIVE_SPACES_PATTERN` regex is `\\s{2,}` (two or more), despite the source comment claiming five or more.

requestBody.description: New user record. `firstName`, `lastName` and `password` must be present (they are trimmed without a null check). `gender` defaults to `others` and `dateOfBirth` to `1990-01-01` when omitted. For `userType=PERSONAL` the part of `kpostID` before `@` must be 4-12 characters.

200.description: Returned for **every** outcome. Success: the service envelope with `status=Success`. Validation failure: `status=Failure`, `statusCode=500`, `errorMsg="Enter valid Credentials"`. Exception: `status=Error`, `statusCode=500`, no `errorMsg`.

400.description: Bean validation on the `User` payload failed, raised before the handler body runs and rendered by `GlobalExceptionHandler`.

401.description: Unauthorized - the `Authorization` header is missing or malformed, the JWT signature is invalid, the access token has expired with no usable refresh token, or the token's `deviceID` claim no longer matches an active login session (for example after a logout from all devices). Re-authenticate to obtain a new token.

403.description: Forbidden - the caller is authenticated but lacks the authority for this route. Applies to `/admin/**` routes that require the `admin` role, and to resource-level checks such as acting on a group the caller does not administer or on a message the caller does not own.

500.description: Internal Server Error - an unhandled exception occurred while servicing the request, typically a MySQL failure, a downstream integration timeout, or object-storage unavailability. The envelope returns `status=Failure` with `statusCode=500`; the stack trace is written to the application log against the caller's kpostID.

post.summary: Set or change a user's access code
post.description:
Stores the access code - the short secondary PIN used to unlock the app and authorise sensitive actions. This is the working replacement for the defective V1 `setAccessCode`.

**Flow.** `UserProfileService.changeAccessCode` updates the access-code column on the user's row in the MySQL user table, returning `Success` when a row was updated. An audit row is written against the payload's `kpostID`.

**Side effects.** Overwrites the stored access code; the previous value is unrecoverable. Because the access code gates in-app unlock, setting it affects every device the user is signed in on.

**Security note - test this explicitly.** The target user is taken **entirely from the request body's `kpostID`**, and this route sits under the `permitAll` `/v2/signupLogin/**` tree, so no bearer token is required and no check ties the payload to an authenticated caller. Unless `UserProfileService.changeAccessCode` performs its own verification - for example requiring the current access code or an OTP - this would allow an unauthenticated caller to overwrite any user's access code given only their `kpostID`, which is an account-takeover vector. QA should attempt exactly that with no `Authorization` header and confirm it is refused; if it succeeds, escalate. Compare `POST /v2/profile/changeOrForgotAccessCode`, which is behind authentication.

**QA notes.** Returns **HTTP 500** whenever the service does not report `Success`, which includes the ordinary "user not found" case. The success envelope carries no `msg` or `data` - only `status`, `statusCode` and `urlPath`.

requestBody.description: The target `kpostID` and the `accessCode` to store. **The user is identified solely by this payload** - see the security note.

200.description: Access code stored. Envelope carries `status=Success`, `statusCode=200` and `urlPath="setAccessCode"`, with no payload.

500.description: The access code was not stored - unknown user, or an exception (`errorValue="Error occured while set Access Code!! "`).

400.description: Bad Request - the JSON body could not be parsed, a mandatory field is missing or empty, or a supplied value failed validation (for example a malformed kpostID, an out-of-range page size, or an unparseable date). The response envelope carries `status=Failure` and a `msg` naming the offending field.

401.description: Unauthorized - the `Authorization` header is missing or malformed, the JWT signature is invalid, the access token has expired with no usable refresh token, or the token's `deviceID` claim no longer matches an active login session (for example after a logout from all devices). Re-authenticate to obtain a new token.

403.description: Forbidden - the caller is authenticated but lacks the authority for this route. Applies to `/admin/**` routes that require the `admin` role, and to resource-level checks such as acting on a group the caller does not administer or on a message the caller does not own.

post.summary: Check kpostID availability and suggest alternatives
post.description:
Checks whether a desired `kpostID` is free during registration and, when it is taken, returns available alternatives in the same response.

**Flow.** The lookup runs **only if** both `firstName` and `lastName` are non-empty after trimming; otherwise `status` stays null and control falls into the taken-branch. When it does run, `SignUpLoginService.isKpostIdExists` queries the MySQL user table. If free, the response is `status=Success` at HTTP 200. If taken, `SignUpLoginService.suggestionList` derives candidates from the name fields and returns the available ones under `data`.

**Side effects.** None - read-only. It does **not** reserve the id, so one reported free can be claimed by another registration before `signup` completes. Writes an audit row against the payload's mobile number.

**Access.** `permitAll` - no bearer token required.

**QA notes.** The status codes are counter-intuitive and worth pinning down: **only the "available" outcome returns HTTP 200**. Both taken-with-suggestions and taken-without-suggestions return **HTTP 500** with `statusCode=500`, even though "this id is taken" is a perfectly normal business answer rather than a server fault. Distinguish them by the presence of `data`. A subtle trap: omitting `firstName`/`lastName` skips the existence check entirely and reports the id as taken regardless of reality - so always send both. Those getters are `.trim()`-ed without a null check, so a missing field throws an NPE caught as the generic 500 with `errorValue="Error while checking KpostID duplication"` and `urlPath` reported as `/isKpostIdExits/`. The misspelling `"already exits!"` is part of the deployed contract.

requestBody.description: The desired `kpostID` plus the name fields. **Both `firstName` and `lastName` are mandatory** - omitting either silently skips the availability check and reports the id as taken.

400.description: Bean validation failed on the `UserRO` payload.

200.description: The kpostID is **available**. Envelope carries `status=Success`, `statusCode=200` and `msg="KpostID is Available. can be used"`.

500.description: The kpostID is **taken** (a normal business outcome, not a fault) or the check could not run. With suggestions: `msg="KpostID is already exits!"` plus `data`. Without: `errorValue`/`errorMsg` and no `data`.

Re-authenticate to obtain a new token.

403.description: Forbidden - the caller is authenticated but lacks the authority for this route. Applies to `/admin/**` routes that require the `admin` role, and to resource-level checks such as acting on a group the caller does not administer or on a message the caller does not own.

post.summary: Generate available kpostID suggestions
post.description:
Returns a set of available `kpostID` candidates derived from the user's name - the "suggest one for me" action on the registration screen.

**Flow.** Guarded identically to `kpostIdExist`: `SignUpLoginService.suggestionList` runs **only if** both `firstName` and `lastName` are non-empty after trimming. It builds candidate ids from those names, checks each against the MySQL user table, and returns only the free ones as a `Set<String>` under `data`.

**Side effects.** None - read-only. Suggestions are **not reserved**, so a returned id may be claimed by another registration before this user completes `signup`; occasional already-taken failures at signup are expected. Writes an audit row against the payload's mobile number.

**Access.** `permitAll` - no bearer token required.

**QA notes.** Because the payload is a `Set`, the array is **unordered and de-duplicated** - never assert on element order or a fixed length. The empty-result case returns **HTTP 500** with `errorMsg="Unable to generate suggestion List! Please Use some other ID."`, which is a normal business answer rather than a fault. Omitting `firstName` or `lastName` skips generation and produces that same 500 - and because both getters are `.trim()`-ed without a null check, a missing field throws an NPE that lands in the catch block with `errorValue="Error while checking and generating suggestion List"` instead. Send both fields.

requestBody.description: Name details used to derive candidates. **Both `firstName` and `lastName` are mandatory.**

200.description: Suggestions generated. Envelope carries `status=Success`, `statusCode=200` and `data` holding the unordered set of available ids.

500.description: No candidates could be generated - either genuinely none are free, or `firstName`/`lastName` were missing. Envelope carries `status=Failure` and an explanatory `errorMsg`.

400.description: Bean validation failed on the `UserRO` payload.

Re-authenticate to obtain a new token.

post.summary: Fetch the caller's login history for a date
post.description:
Returns the signed-in user's historical sign-in records for a selected date - the security-review screen that lets someone check when and from which devices their account was accessed, distinct from `getActiveSession`, which shows only sessions that are still live.

**Flow.** `SignUpLoginService.getLoginHistory` is called with the `kpostID` resolved from the bearer token and the `selectedDate` taken from the request body, selecting the matching rows from the MySQL login-history table. An audit row is written.

**Side effects.** None - read-only.

**QA notes.** Identity comes from the token and only the date comes from the body, so cross-user reads are not possible here - a useful contrast with the V1 session endpoints. `selectedDate` is read via `requestMap.get("selectedDate")` and cast to `String`: sending a non-string JSON value (a number, or a nested object) raises a `ClassCastException` that is caught and reported as the generic **HTTP 500**, so always send it as a quoted string in the format the service expects (`yyyy-MM-dd`). Omitting the key entirely passes null through to the service. A date with no sign-ins returns the empty case as **HTTP 500** with `status=Failure` - treat that as "no records" rather than a fault. Note `userSessionList.isEmpty()` is called without a null check.

requestBody.description: Carries `selectedDate` as a **quoted string** (`yyyy-MM-dd`). The user is taken from the bearer token, not from this payload.

200.description: Login history retrieved. Envelope carries `status=Success`, `statusCode=200` and `data` holding the array of `LoginHistory` records.

500.description: No sign-in records exist for that date, `selectedDate` was not a JSON string, or the lookup failed. Envelope carries `status=Failure` and `statusCode=500`.

400.description: Bad Request - the JSON body could not be parsed, a mandatory field is missing or empty, or a supplied value failed validation (for example a malformed kpostID, an out-of-range page size, or an unparseable date). The response envelope carries `status=Failure` and a `msg` naming the offending field.

post.summary: Exchange a refresh token for a new access token
post.description:
Mints a fresh JWT access token from a still-valid refresh token, letting a client stay signed in without prompting the user for credentials again.

**Flow.** `SignUpLoginServiceV2.generateJWTokens` validates the supplied refresh token's signature and expiry, confirms the associated `deviceID` still has a live row in the MySQL login-session table, and issues a new access token carrying the same `kpostID`, `deviceID` and `companyID` claims. The service composes the entire response, which is returned unchanged.

**Side effects.** No new session row is created - the existing one is reused - though last-activity timestamps may be touched. Depending on the service's rotation policy the refresh token may itself be rotated, in which case the client must store the new one.

**Access.** `permitAll` - deliberately so, since the caller's access token has by definition expired at this point. The refresh token is the sole credential, which makes it as sensitive as a password: it must be stored securely and never logged.

**QA notes.** The important negative cases are an expired refresh token, a malformed or tampered token, and - the security-relevant one - a refresh token whose session has been revoked via `userLogoutFromAllDevices`. That last case **must** fail: if a revoked session can still mint access tokens, logout is ineffective. Note this route is a distinct mechanism from the filter-level refresh described on the API description, where presenting an expired access token alongside a valid refresh token causes `AuthenticationFilter` to return a new token in the `Authorization` **response header**; both paths should be covered. Failures inside the service produce its own envelope, while an exception escaping it yields `status=Error` with `errorMsg`.

500.description: The refresh token was invalid, expired, or its session has been revoked. Envelope carries `statusCode=500`, `status=Error` and `errorMsg`.

200.description: A new access token was issued. The body is the service layer's envelope carrying the token (and possibly a rotated refresh token).

400.description: Bad Request - the JSON body could not be parsed, a mandatory field is missing or empty, or a supplied value failed validation (for example a malformed kpostID, an out-of-range page size, or an unparseable date). The response envelope carries `status=Failure` and a `msg` naming the offending field.

Re-authenticate to obtain a new token.

post.summary: Fetch a user's name and designation
post.description:
Returns the display name and job designation for a user - the lightweight identity lookup used to render name chips during invite, search and sign-up flows without loading a full profile.

**Flow.** A pure pass-through: `SignUpLoginService.fetchNameAndDesignation` reads the lookup keys from the untyped request map and selects the name and designation columns, joining the user and designation reference tables in MySQL. The service builds the entire envelope; this handler only inspects its `status` to choose between HTTP 200 and 500. An audit row is written against the payload's `kpostID`.

**Side effects.** None - read-only.

**Security note.** The subject is taken from the request body and the route is `permitAll`, so this is reachable **without a bearer token**. It exposes a user's real name and designation to anyone who can guess or enumerate a `kpostID`. QA should confirm whether the service honours the target user's profile-privacy settings; if it does not, this is an unauthenticated information-disclosure and enumeration vector worth raising. Compare `POST /v2/profile/getUserBasicDetailsUsingKpostID`, which sits behind authentication.

**QA notes.** There is **no try/catch** - an exception inside the service escapes to `GlobalExceptionHandler` rather than producing this route's envelope. The handler also calls `result.get(STATUS)` without a null check, so a service returning a null map would NPE. Any outcome where `status` is not exactly `Success` maps to **HTTP 500**, including "user not found". Note the audit action is logged as `/fetchUserDetails`.

post.description:
Returns identity details for a user on the **personal** account tier, as opposed to the company-linked enterprise tier served by `fetchUserDetails`. Personal accounts have no company or designation, so this variant returns the personal-profile fields instead.

**Flow.** A pure pass-through to `SignUpLoginService.fetchPersonalUserDetails`, which reads the lookup keys from the untyped request map and selects the personal-account columns from the MySQL user and profile tables. The service composes the whole envelope; this handler only inspects `status` to choose between HTTP 200 and 500. An audit row is written against the payload's `kpostID`.

**Side effects.** None - read-only.

**Security note.** Carries the same exposure as `fetchUserDetails`: the subject comes from the request body, and the route is `permitAll`, so it is reachable **without a bearer token** and can be used to enumerate personal accounts by `kpostID`. Confirm whether the service honours the target user's privacy settings.

**QA notes.** No try/catch - exceptions escape to `GlobalExceptionHandler`; and `result.get(STATUS)` is dereferenced without a null check. Any `status` other than `Success` maps to **HTTP 500**, including "user not found" and, notably, the case where the `kpostID` exists but belongs to an **enterprise** account rather than a personal one - use `fetchUserDetails` for those. The audit action for this route is logged as `/fetchUserDetails` (a copy-paste artefact), so the audit trail cannot distinguish the two endpoints.

post.summary: Register a company administrator account
post.description:
Creates the administrator account for a company - the onboarding path that establishes the first privileged user, who can then provision staff through `AdminController`.

**Flow.** An audit row is written against the payload's mobile number. The handler checks only that `kpostID` is non-empty, then delegates to `SignUpLoginService.adminRegistration`, which validates uniqueness, creates or links the company record, inserts the user with the **admin role** granted, and writes the profile and default-settings rows in MySQL. The service returns its own `ResponseEntity`, which is passed through unchanged - so the success-path status code originates in the service, not here.

**Side effects.** Creates a privileged account and, typically, a company record; dispatches onboarding credentials by SMS/email. The account created here can subsequently reach every `/admin/**` route, which is role-gated behind `hasRole("admin")`.

**Security note - test this explicitly.** This route sits under the `permitAll` `/v2/signupLogin/**` tree, so **no bearer token and no existing admin privilege is required to create an administrator**. The only controller-level check is that `kpostID` is non-empty. Whether that is acceptable depends entirely on verification inside `SignUpLoginService.adminRegistration` - for example requiring an OTP-verified mobile number, an invitation token, or rejecting a `companyID` that already has an admin. QA should attempt to register an admin against an **existing** company with no token and confirm it is refused; if it succeeds, that is a privilege-escalation path into another organisation's data and should be escalated immediately.

**QA notes.** The empty-`kpostID` branch is one of the few genuine **400** responses in the codebase. Note it reports `status=Error` (not `Failure`) with `errorMsg="Enter valid KpostID"`. Unlike `signup`, this route applies no format checks on `kpostID` beyond non-emptiness - no `@` requirement, no length rule - so those are the service's responsibility.

post.summary: Upload supporting attachments to the caller's profile
post.description: Uploads one or more supporting documents to the signed-in user's profile - typically certificates, qualification proofs or portfolio items backing the education and experience sections. A **multipart/form-data** endpoint accepting an **array** of files in a single request. Each file is streamed to S3 under a key scoped by the caller's `kpostID` from the bearer token, and the resulting paths are recorded against the profile in MySQL. Side effects: stores objects in S3, counts against the user's storage quota (see `getStorageDetails`), and makes the documents retrievable. QA notes: this is the only route in the controller taking a **file array**, so test the batch semantics explicitly - in particular whether one bad file in a batch aborts the whole upload or is skipped while the rest succeed, and how partial success is reported. Also test the empty array, a single file, and enough files to exceed the container's multipart limits. Because these may be identity documents, confirm what access control applies when they are later retrieved - if they are served from a `permitAll` path like the profile images, that would be a significant disclosure risk worth escalating.

post.description: Uploads an image to S3 and returns the stored object reference - a general-purpose helper rather than a route tied to a specific profile field, used when a client needs an image stored before associating it with something else. Side effects: writes an object to S3 and consumes storage. QA notes - **two defects to check**. First, the file parameter is annotated `@RequestBody MultipartFile` rather than `@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile`, which is the form used by every other upload route in this controller. `@RequestBody` on a `MultipartFile` is not the conventional binding and may fail to resolve a standard `multipart/form-data` request - **verify this endpoint actually accepts a normal multipart upload at all** before writing tests around it; it may be effectively broken. Second, the handler takes no `HttpServletRequest`, so no caller identity reaches the service - establish which S3 prefix the object lands in and whether an authenticated user could write outside their own namespace. Also confirm content-type validation and size limits. Prefer the purpose-specific upload routes (`updateProfileImage`, `uploadCoverImage`, `uploadProfileAttachments`) over this one.

post.summary: [Maintenance] Kmail password remediation patch
post.description:
A **maintenance/remediation endpoint**, not part of the normal client flow - the name `patchWork` marks it as a one-off fix-up routine added to repair Kmail password state for affected accounts, most likely following a migration or defect. It writes Kmail credential state via the Kmail schema (`Schema3ConfigKMail`) rather than the primary KPOST datasource.

**Side effects - credential-modifying.** This alters Kmail passwords, so it can change or reset authentication state for the accounts it touches. Depending on the payload's scope it may affect **multiple users in one call**, which makes it considerably more dangerous than the ordinary self-service password routes.

**Security note - the key question for QA.** This route carries **no role gate**: it sits on `/v2/profile`, which requires authentication but not the `admin` authority that `SecurityConfiguration` applies to `/admin/**`. A maintenance routine that modifies credentials should not be reachable by an ordinary authenticated user. Establish exactly whose credentials it can alter and whether the service restricts it; if a normal user can invoke it against other accounts, **escalate**. Strongly consider whether it should be removed from the deployed API altogether now that its remediation purpose has presumably been served.

**QA notes.** Do not exercise against shared environments. The `UserGroupRO` payload type suggests it may operate over a group or list of users - confirm the blast radius before invoking. Its presence in the published spec is itself worth flagging to the team.

post.summary: Fetch another user's profile by kpostID
post.description:
Returns the profile of the user named in the request body - the read behind viewing someone else's profile from a contact list, search result or group member list.

**Flow.** `UserProfileService` resolves the profile for the supplied `kpostID` from the MySQL user, profile, education and experience tables.

**Side effects.** None - read-only.

**Security note - privacy filtering is an acknowledged gap.** The source carries the inline comment `/* Need to validate based on privacy setting */` on this mapping, which is the authors' own record that the privacy check is **not yet implemented here**. The subject is taken entirely from the request body and the caller's identity is not passed to the service, so the privacy flags a user sets through `setProfilePrivacy` and `updatePrivacySettingDetails` are likely **not honoured** on this route. Any authenticated user may therefore be able to retrieve another user's full profile - including fields explicitly marked private - simply by supplying their `kpostID`.

**This is the highest-priority test in the controller.** As user B, hide contact details via `setProfilePrivacy`; then as user A call this route for B and assert the hidden fields are absent. If they are returned, this is a confirmed privacy-control bypass affecting every user on the platform, and should be escalated rather than filed as a documentation note. Also compare against `getUserBasicDetailsUsingKpostID`, which returns a deliberately narrower field set and may be the safer route for third-party reads.

**QA notes.** `kpostID` is unvalidated, so an unknown id returns the failure envelope rather than a 404. Being body-driven, this route is also usable to enumerate which kpostIDs exist.

post.summary: Deactivate the caller's account
post.description:
Deactivates the signed-in user's KPOST account after the OTP issued by `sendAccountDeactivationOtp` has been verified. The account is resolved from the bearer token, so a caller can only deactivate their own; the supplied reason and OTP are recorded and the account is marked deactivated in MySQL.

**Side effects - the most destructive user-initiated action in the API.** The user can no longer sign in; live sessions should be revoked; the account disappears from search and contact lists; and depending on retention policy, messages, attachments and group memberships may be purged or anonymised. Whether this is reversible - and by whom - is a service-layer decision that must be established and documented, since there is **no reactivation endpoint in this API**.

**QA notes.** Exercise on disposable test accounts only. The critical security test is that deactivation **cannot** proceed without a valid OTP: attempt it with no OTP, a wrong OTP, an expired OTP, and a replayed one, and confirm each is refused. Then verify the consequences: a token issued before deactivation must stop authenticating, the user must vanish from `advancedSearch`, and other users' contact lists should reflect the change. Confirm the storage the account consumed is released or retained per policy.

post.summary: Change the caller's password

Changes the signed-in user's password after verifying the current one. **This is the safe replacement for `POST /profile/changePassword`**, which took the target account from the request body with no ownership check; here the account is resolved from the bearer token, so a caller can only ever change their own password.

Any `kpostID` in the body is irrelevant; confirm that supplying another user's id does **not** redirect the change. A wrong current password returns the failure envelope with a real HTTP 500, not the silent empty body the V1 route produced.
